newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn retreats from gold grab after politicians balk.
newsitem.headline: Bonn retreats from gold grab after politicians balk.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government retreated Tuesday from a controversial plan to revalue central bank gold reserves after members of parliament from Kohl's party balked at the widely scorned plan.

Sources in Kohl's centre-right coalition said the government had abandoned its plan to reap billions of marks (dollars) in quick cash profits from the Bundesbank this year and would instead accept the central bank's offer to transfer the funds in 1998.

The humbling retreat will make it harder for Germany to qualify for Europe's single currency because Bonn badly needed the 10 billion marks ($5.8 billion) from the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves to help it qualify.
The criteria agreed for participation in a single European currency pinpoint 1997 as the critical year for measuring government budget deficits to see who will qualify to join in 1999.

But Bonn's decision to back down amid withering criticism from the Bundesbank is likely to fortify Europe's economic and monetary union in the long run as the move is certain to restore public confidence in the so-called "euro" currency.
"A solution is only possible with support of the Bundesbank," the coalition source said. "In face of the resistance from the Bundesbank, the revaluation for 1997 is no longer on the table."

Abandoning the plan to revalue the assets will mean that the hole in Bonn's 1997 budget will be bigger by 10 billion mark ($5.8 billion), the official said. To fill that hole, the coalition is discussing privatisations, budget cuts and tax increases.

The agreement emerged after Finance Minister Theo Waigel and Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer met in Bonn for what was supposed to be a secret negotiation. Scores of journalists appeared at the Finance Ministry once word spread that Tietmeyer had arrived.
"We had good talks and we are on the way to an agreement," Waigel said after the 30-minute meeting.
"We are indeed," Tietmeyer added. "I hope that we can come to an agreement."
They declined to provide further details and walked quickly away.
Moments later, coalition sources confirmed Bonn was retreating.

The central bank was not opposed in principle to revaluing its gold reserves but insisted that the process should not take place until 1999 -- or at least not before the May 1998 decision on who will participate in monetary union.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks ($7.9 billion) -- compared with a current market value of more than 55 billion marks ($31.8 billion).

The government's unprecedented grab for the gold had stunned the Bundesbank and raised eyebrows throughout Europe, especially in countries to which German officials had long been delivering stern lectures against such budgetary sleight-of-hand.
Members of the German parliament had seemed surprised by the Bundesbank's firm rejection of the plan as many apparently assumed that Waigel had first won central bank backing.
The fiercely independent Bundesbank enjoys wide respect in Germany and many politicians were clearly loath to take on the institution.
The Bundesbank sternly warned Bonn against resorting to tricks designed to squeeze Germany into Europe's currency union.

Angered by Waigel's plan to revalue reserves and use a part of those proceeds to fill budget holes this year, the Bundesbank compared Bonn's plans to practices which Bonn itself had disapproved of when proposed by other governments.
